The '''Cyatheaceae''' are a [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] of [[Polypodiophyta|ferns]], the scaly tree ferns, one of eight families in the order [[Cyatheales]] in the [[Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group]] classification of 2016 (PPG I).<ref name=PPGI/> Alternatively, the family may defined much more broadly (Cyatheaceae ''[[sensu|sensu lato]]'') as the only family in the Cyatheales, with the PPG I family treated as the subfamily '''Cyatheoideae'''.<ref name=ChriChas14/> The narrower [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscription]] is used in this article.

The family includes the world's tallest tree ferns, which reach heights up to 20 m. They are also very ancient plants, appearing in the [[fossil]] record in the [[late Jurassic]], though the modern [[genus|genera]] likely appeared in the [[Cenozoic]]. Cyatheaceae are the largest family of tree ferns, including about 640 species.<ref name=PPGI/> Cyatheaceae and [[Dicksoniaceae]], together with [[Metaxyaceae]] and [[Cibotiaceae]], do not form a strongly supported monophyletic group and could be paraphyletic, but several individual subgroups are well supported as being monophyletic. Cyatheaceae are [[leptosporangiate ferns]], the most familiar group of [[monilophyte]]s.<ref name=KoraConaMetzSchn07/>

The Cyatheaceae usually have a single, erect or creeping  [[rhizome]] (stem).  Their fronds (leaves) are also very large, although not as large as the tree ferns of the [[Marattiaceae]]. Some species have fronds reaching 3–4 m in length, and have a final crown width of some 6 m. The fronds are [[vernation|circinate]] before unfolding and usually [[pinnate]]ly or bipinnately compound, with deeply pinnately lobed [[leaflet (botany)|leaflets]]. The large leaves are covered in scales and hairs, and bear [[sorus|sori]] (spore clusters) on their undersides.<ref name="Judd 2008">Judd, W.S., C.S. Campbell, E.A. Kellogg, P.F. Stevens, and M.J. Donoghue (Eds.) 2008. Plant Systematics: A Phylogenetic Approach, Third Edition. Sinauer Associates, Sunderland, Massachusetts, USA.</ref> The sori are often covered by a flap of tissue called an indusium, a useful characteristic for classifying the Cyatheaceae. Some indusia are cup-shaped (cyatheoid), while others are hood-shaped (hemitelioid), enclose the sorus (sphaeropteroid), or scaly. Like most ferns, members of the Cyatheaceae are homosporous. Cyatheaceae are found in both New and Old World tropical wet montane forests and [[cloud forest]]s, with some species extending into south-temperate regions.<ref name=KoraConaMetzSchn07/> Most Cyatheaceae are terrestrial, with one being a facultative [[epiphyte]] and others having a creeping habit.

[[File:Long Bao Valley Cyatheaceae.jpg|thumb]]

Cyatheaceae can be distinguished from arborescent ''[[Dicksonia]]'' by the presence of scales, the position of the [[Sorus|sori]], and the morphology of [[sporangia]] and [[spores]].<ref name="Holttum and Edwards 1983">Holttum, R.E. and P.J. Edwards. 1983. The tree-ferns of Mount Roraima and neighbouring areas of the Guayana highlands with comments on the family Cyatheaceae. Kew Bulletin 38(2): 155-188.</ref> In the Cyatheaceae, the sori occur away from the margins of the pinnules, and are elongate or rounded.

==Taxonomy==
{{As of|2019}}, two different [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscriptions]] of the family Cyatheaceae are used, as summarized in the table below. In the [[Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group]] classification of 2016 (PPG I), the family is one of eight in the order Cyatheales, and has three genera.<ref name=PPGI/> In the classification of Christenhusz & Chase (2014), the family is the only one in the order Cytheales, the families of PPG I being reduced to subfamilies. It then has 13–14 genera.<ref name=ChriChas14/> The ''[[Sensu|sensu stricto]]'' circumscription of PPG I is used here.

===Genera===
Since the exact number of species is not known, classification of the Cyatheaceae ''s.s.'' has had a long and controversial history, and is still undergoing revision. Three tentative [[clade]]s have been developed: ''Alsophila'', ''Cyathea'', and ''Sphaeropteris''. These are frequently used as genus names. ''Cnemidaria'', ''Trichopteris'' (or ''Trichipteris''), and ''Nephelea'' (or ''Nephelia'') have also been suggested as genera. Initially, indusium and scale [[morphology (biology)|morphology]] were used to organize the Cyatheaceae into [[taxonomic rank]]s. Most recently, [[plastid]] [[DNA]] has been used, suggesting the Cyatheaceae should be split into four [[clade]]s: ''[[Sphaeropteris]]'', ''[[Cyathea]]'', ''[[Alsophila (plant)|Alsophila]]'', and ''Gymnosphaera + A. capensis''. {{As of|2007}}, it remained unclear which of these groups should be considered genera and which subgenera.<ref name=KoraConaMetzSchn07/>

The [[Pteridophyte Phylogeny Group]] classification of 2016 (PPG I) accepts three genera, placing the ''Gymnosphaera'' clade within ''Alsophila'':<ref name=PPGI/>
* ''[[Alsophila (plant)|Alsophila]]'' <small>R.Br.</small>, about 275 species
* ''[[Cyathea]]'' <small>Sm.</small>, about 265 species
* ''[[Sphaeropteris]]'' <small>Bernh.</small>, about 103 species
